article.overview: A laser absorption spectrometer identifies and measures gases by passing laser light through a gas sample and recording how strongly each gas absorbs light at particular wavelengths. Each gas species absorbs at its own characteristic wavelengths, so the pattern of absorption works as a molecular fingerprint [1][2]. The catalogue places this payload in the lunar exosphere and atmospheric instruments category. The two lunar-oriented examples identified in public sources, however, are designed to analyse gases released when a regolith or surface sample is heated, not to measure the thin lunar exosphere directly [1][3]. No laser absorption spectrometer designed specifically for the lunar exosphere was identified during this research, so this article describes a payload class with examples rather than a flown or selected exosphere instrument.
article.description: The payload class uses a tunable laser, a gas cell or optical path, and a detector. The laser is tuned to wavelengths where the target gas absorbs. The amount of light lost on passing through the gas is related to the concentration of that gas. In the SwRI design for LASVEGAS, the gas flows into a small cylindrical chamber where the laser light reflects between mirrors at each end, lengthening the optical path through the sample [1][2]. The Russian DLS-L is described as a tunable diode laser spectrometer [3]. The absorption technique behind that name is inferred from the instrument name, because the abstract page does not state the measurement principle explicitly [3]. A later journal version of the DLS-L work is indicated by DOI 10.1016/j.pss.2024.105935 [4]. That journal article was not opened during this research.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a laser absorption spectrometer is quantitative, species-specific gas measurement. For surface-volatile work, the targets reported for the two examples are water and other volatiles such as methane in gases released from heated samples [1][2]. For DLS-L, the stated targets are isotope ratios, including D/H, 18O/17O/16O and 13C/12C, in volatiles released from lunar regolith [3]. Water is named as a mission objective for the Luna-27 lander, but the abstract does not list H2O as a directly measured species [3]. The SwRI description also refers to measuring gases from planetary atmospheres, such as Mars [1][2]. Applications in the lunar exosphere or thin atmosphere would need a different design and sampling approach. No source identified in this research establishes such an application.
article.operating_principle: A typical laser absorption spectrometer follows this sequence. A gas sample enters an optical cell; for surface-volatile instruments, the gas is released by heating a small regolith or planetary sample [1][2]. Laser light at selected wavelengths passes through the gas, and in the LASVEGAS design it is reflected between mirrors, which increases the path length through the gas [1][2]. Each gas absorbs light at its own wavelengths, producing a species-specific signature, and a detector measures the remaining intensity [1][2]. The measured absorption is converted into gas abundance; for isotope analysis, the instrument compares absorption lines of different isotopologues [3]. The operating principle is described qualitatively in the sources reviewed. No published laser wavelengths, path lengths or calibration values were found for either example.
article.scientific_importance: The main scientific value of a laser absorption spectrometer lies in quantitative, species-specific gas measurements, including isotope ratios that can distinguish closely related molecules. For the Luna-27 DLS-L, the stated measurement targets are isotope ratios such as D/H, 18O/17O/16O and 13C/12C in volatiles released from lunar regolith [3]. Such measurements can inform questions about the origin and storage of lunar volatiles, which is a general scientific rationale rather than a result from the cited sources. No published result from either example instrument was identified, so the scientific importance described here is a stated objective rather than an achieved outcome.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a laser absorption spectrometer. Designs differ widely in optical layout, laser type, sample handling and maturity. The two examples below are specific development instruments, not every instrument in this class. Neither has published mass, power, detection-limit or laser-wavelength values in the sources reviewed, so those values are recorded as null rather than estimated.

examples.name: LASVEGAS (Laser Absorption Spectrometer for Volatiles and Evolved Gas)
examples.type: Engineering development for lunar surface operation; not flown
examples.flight_status: Not flown. SwRI states the instrument is yet to be selected for flight on a mission.
examples.heritage: NASA MatISSE programme provided $3 million in 2019 for an icy-worlds version; the DALI programme provided a further $3 million in 2020 to adapt the design for lunar surface operation.
examples.dimensions_description: SwRI describes the instrument as about half the size of a paper towel roll. No dimensions are published.
examples.measurement: Heated sample gas flows into a cylindrical chamber where laser light reflects between mirrors; absorption is measured to identify and quantify species, including water and methane.
examples.trl: Not verified. One search summary cites a TRL 6 maturation target; a less authoritative source gives TRL 4. Neither was verified on a primary source.

examples.name: DLS-L (Diode Laser Spectrometer), Luna-27 lander
examples.type: Proposed flight instrument for the Luna-27 lander; not flown
examples.flight_status: Proposed. The Luna-27 lander is planned to land at the lunar south pole in 2028, per the arXiv abstract.
examples.dimensions_description: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.measurement: Isotope ratios D/H, 18O/17O/16O and 13C/12C in volatiles evolved from regolith.
examples.gas_analysis_package_context: Secondary search summaries describe DLS-L as one of three instruments with a thermal analyser (TA-L), a gas chromatograph (GC-L) and a neutral gas mass spectrometer (NGMS). The primary source for this arrangement was not read and is not verified.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No dimensions are published for either example. LASVEGAS is described qualitatively as about half the size of a paper towel roll [1]. DLS-L dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not publicly specified for either example. Values recorded as null.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Described qualitatively as low power for LASVEGAS [1]; no numeric value is published. DLS-L power is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: No environmental qualification or operating-range values were published in the sources reviewed for either example. General engineering considerations, which are not source-specific, include temperature control of the gas cell and sample-heating chamber, clean and sealed gas handling to avoid contamination, and power and thermal management during heating cycles. These are not stated requirements for any named instrument.
article.limitations: Exosphere relevance: neither example is documented as measuring the lunar exosphere; their stated use is analysis of gases released from heated samples [1][3]. Sample-release dependence: measurements made on heated samples describe volatiles released under heating and do not represent ambient gas in the environment [1][3]. Unverified performance: laser wavelengths, sensitivity, precision and mass/power values are not published for either example [1][3]. Conflicting species descriptions: one search summary says DLS-L tracks H2O and CO2 concentration dynamics, whereas the primary abstract names isotope ratios and lists water only as a mission objective [3]; this conflict was not resolved. Maturity and schedule: LASVEGAS has no flight selection [1], and the Luna-27 schedule varies between sources.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The sources reviewed do not specify the Earth integration, launch, lunar transfer, landing delivery, deployment steps, power and data interfaces, or thermal and mechanical interfaces for either example. No interface evidence was found that would support a compatibility claim.
transportation_process: Earth integration of the instrument into a lander or spacecraft: not publicly specified for either example.
Launch and lunar transfer: not publicly specified for either example; DLS-L is planned for the Luna-27 lander [3].
Landing delivery at the lunar surface: DLS-L is planned for a south-pole landing in 2028 [3]; LASVEGAS has no documented lander or rover integration.

Deployment and sample handling: DLS-L integration with the lander's sample-handling system is not verified; secondary search summaries describe robotic-arm loading of regolith into a thermal analyser, not confirmed from a primary source.
Power, data, thermal and mechanical interfaces: not publicly specified for either example.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not publicly specified for either example. LASVEGAS is described as compact [1][2], but no deployment method is documented in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No flown lunar example of a laser absorption spectrometer for this payload class was identified. The LASVEGAS and DLS-L development programmes are the closest documented examples [1][3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with a named lander or rover is not asserted. An assessment would require published mass, dimensions, mounting interfaces, power and data requirements, and deployment or sampling constraints.

article.historical_significance: Laser absorption spectroscopy is an established method for gas measurement in laboratory and field settings; its use in lunar work is more recent. LASVEGAS is notable as an example of a planetary volatile instrument adapted from an icy-worlds concept (MatISSE) to a lunar surface design (DALI) [1]. The DLS-L is notable as a Russian lunar instrument intended to analyse volatiles from regolith with isotope-ratio measurements [3]. A conference paper on a multichannel version of DLS-L is listed in SPIE Proceedings under DOI 10.1117/12.2602144 [5]; that paper's abstract was not accessible, so its contents are not summarised here.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The limitations are significant and mainly reflect the state of public evidence. Neither example instrument has a published mass, power, detection limit or laser wavelength range in the sources reviewed, and no flight selection or flight heritage was confirmed for either. Measurements made on heated samples describe volatiles released under heating and do not represent the ambient exosphere. Sources also disagree on whether DLS-L measures water and carbon dioxide concentrations directly or primarily reports isotope ratios, and this was not resolved from the primary abstract. Schedule information for Luna-27 also varies between sources.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image assets were verified for this payload, so no image objects are included; the SwRI news page image was not used because it could not be confirmed to show the instrument.

data_quality_notes: No exosphere-specific laser absorption spectrometer was identified. The two examples are surface-volatile gas instruments; the catalogue category (lunar exosphere and atmospheric instruments) is retained as given.
No mass, power, dimensions, laser wavelength range, precision or detection-limit values are published in the sources reviewed for LASVEGAS or DLS-L; all such values are null.
LASVEGAS TRL is not verified: one search summary cites a TRL 6 target and a less authoritative source gives TRL 4.
DLS-L species description conflicts between a search summary (H2O and CO2 concentration dynamics) and the primary arXiv abstract (isotope ratios; water as a mission objective). Unresolved.
DLS-L Gas Analysis Package composition (TA-L, GC-L, NGMS) and the regolith-loading sequence come from secondary search summaries and are not verified against a primary source.
The DLS-L full PDF, the journal version (DOI 10.1016/j.pss.2024.105935) and the SPIE paper (DOI 10.1117/12.2602144) were not readable through the tools used.
No image assets were verified for this payload. Image arrays are empty by design.
Luna-27 schedule (2028 south-pole landing) is taken from the arXiv abstract; a separate older source gave an earlier timeframe and current 2026 status was not verified.
